issues.passage: As the deadline approached, the team's anxiety only seemed to subside with every new complication.
issues.why: "Anxiety ... seemed to subside" is valid, natural use of subside = become less intense. The deadline/complications framing is only pragmatically odd; it does not make the verb a misuse. A student who knows the definition would rightly accept this passage.

fix.correctPassage: Once the fever began to subside, she was able to sleep through the night.
wrongPassages: Managers hoped a larger bonus would subside employees who had threatened to walk out.
The city council voted to subside the after-school music program that parents had long supported.
She planned to subside the quiet research post for a louder role in public affairs.

issues.passage: The open forum was designed to preclude neighbors who had felt shut out of earlier planning meetings.
issues.why: "Preclude neighbors" is usable as prevent/rule out those people (from taking part). That matches preclude = make impossible / prevent. Calling the event an "open forum" is only pragmatically odd; the word itself is not misused.

fix.correctPassage: A prior commitment precludes her from joining the evening session.
wrongPassages: Her brief remarks will preclude the keynote and establish the themes for the rest of the day.
The signed form will preclude that every volunteer has read the safety guidelines.
Weekend clinics preclude free screenings to residents who lack insurance.

issues.passage: Flexible office hours preclude students who need help outside the standard schedule.
issues.why: "X precludes students who..." is the same preventive construction as in correct usage (e.g. rigid rules preclude students who work days). Flexible hours making that claim is only situationally inverted; the verb is still used as prevent, not as a clear misuse.
